wa_northwest_ridge_2.rappels: 3–5 rappels on the ridge itself to get past its gendarmes, off threaded cord rather than fixed stations; the way off the summit is the standard rappel line down the south side, shared with the Southeast Face route
wa_northwest_ridge_2.approach: There is no standalone approach described for this ridge. What is confirmed is that the ridge connecting Boston Peak toward Forbidden Peak passes over Sharkfin Tower (8,120+ ft), and the only known ascent reached it via a multi-day connecting traverse begun on Forbidden Peak rather than as a direct approach to Boston. For a party attempting it directly, the most logical line mirrors the standard access used for the Forbidden/Torment/Sharkfin ridge system: from the Cascade River Road pullout just past mile marker 22 (across from Johannesburg Mountain), follow the old mining road about 0.75 mile to the historic mine site, then the steep, eroded Boston Basin climbers' path — with four stream crossings — up through forest to treeline near 5,300 ft. Boston Basin proper sits at ~5,700 ft, with a low camp around 5,300 ft and a high camp around 6,400 ft. From high camp, glacier travel up the Quien Sabe/Boston Glacier basin toward the col between Sharkfin Tower and Boston would put a party at the low (southwest) end of this ridge; from there the crest itself has no published route description, so expect sustained, likely-loose 4th-class-or-harder ridge climbing with route-finding as the real crux. Treat this as a reasoned estimate from the area's standard access pattern, not confirmed beta for this specific line.

wa_south_ridge_4.rappels: Several rappels used to bypass gendarmes along the ridge crest

wa_austera_peak.beta: From Eldorado camp, traverse the Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col, pass through the col, and follow the north ridge along the McAllister Glacier to a break at about 7,900 ft, where climbers rappel 75 ft to the Klawatti Glacier. From there, 4th and easy 5th class climbing for about 150 ft gains the sub-summit; a further short pitch (roughly 50 ft, reported as well-protected 5.5) on the loose summit tower reaches the true summit.

wa_fortress_mountain_east_ridge.approach: From Trinity Trailhead, hike the Chiwawa River Trail (#1550) north along the valley, passing beneath Red Mountain, to around 6,580 ft, then leave the trail to traverse diagonally up toward Chiwawa Mountain's east ridge, descending to the roughly 7,200 ft col between Chiwawa and Fortress (or continuing over Chiwawa's summit first). Some parties instead approach via the Red Mountain Trail and Chiwawa Basin, fording the Chiwawa River. From the col, a loose class 3-4 gully gains the crest of Fortress's East Ridge.
wa_fortress_mountain_east_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, down-climb the exposed 4th-class step and follow the East Ridge crest back to the head of the loose gully, descending it carefully to the ~7,200 ft col. From the col, either continue on to Chiwawa Mountain (a common combined objective) or drop back to the ~6,580 ft bench and retrace the cross-country line down to the Chiwawa River Trail, then out via the Buck Creek Trail to Trinity Trailhead.
wa_fortress_mountain_east_ridge.overview: A cross-country approach via the Chiwawa River drainage to the col between Chiwawa Mountain and Fortress, then a loose gully gaining Fortress's East Ridge, followed by better-quality ridge scrambling to an exposed 4th-class step just below the summit.

wa_big_four_mountain_spindrift_couloir.beta: First climbed March 2, 1996 by Bart Paull and Doug Littauer in a fast, ultralight, ~9-hour push with no bivy gear. The route starts up an 'ice ribbon' on the initial slabs (roughly 75-degree névé and water ice), continues through the main couloir's three steps of mostly moderate terrain, and hits its crux about three-quarters height: a 100-foot pitch of near-vertical ice leading to steep, often runnelled snow. The upper section mixes rotten ice, shale, and drytooling moves up to roughly 95-degree angles before summit cornices, which may require tunneling through.

wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.beta: From the base glacier, Ptarmigan Ridge climbs an ice step at the bergschrund onto a roughly 1,000 ft rising traverse of 50-60° alpine ice, through sections of waterfall ice (WI3), to a crux rock chimney (5.6, often ice-filled to WI3) around 12,000-12,200 ft; technical climbing eases above this into snow slopes leading up to Liberty Cap. Liberty Wall's serac looms directly above parts of the route and is the primary objective hazard.

wa_lane_peak_r3.overview: The steepest and narrowest of Lane Peak's three north-face couloirs, climbing sustained 40-60° snow/ice to a notch above and left of the Zipper, then rappelling into the Zipper for the descent/summit finish.
wa_lane_peak_r3.beta: This alpine ice/snow route ascends a north-facing couloir just left (climber's) of the Zipper, with two or three steeper sections requiring ice protection along the way, topping out on a ridge above the Zipper route. From the top, climbers typically rappel 100+ ft (double rope recommended) into the adjacent Zipper couloir before traversing to the summit or continuing the descent.
wa_lane_peak_r3.descent_text: Most parties make a single rappel of 100+ ft (a 70m rope allows some downclimbing on moderate snow first, but the rappel itself is usually longer than 100 ft, so a double-rope rappel is recommended) from the ridge top into the adjacent Zipper couloir, then either downclimb the remaining Zipper snow to the base or continue over to the standard South Face line and the Lane-Denman saddle to reach the true summit and descend.
wa_lane_peak_r3.rappels: One roughly 100+ ft rappel (double rope recommended) from the ridge top into the adjacent Zipper couloir

wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.descent_text: Rappel the route on gear from the top of the second pitch — quickest and simplest. If you continue to the top of The Monk, descend the northeast gully with three 75-foot rappels, each covered by a doubled 60 m rope; carry webbing and rings since the anchors are not documented as fixed. From the base, walk down the talus and slabs and follow the drainage back to Upper Cathedral Lake in 30–40 minutes.
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack.rappels: Three 75-ft rappels down the northeast gully if you continue to the top of The Monk; otherwise rappel the route

wa_ne_ridge.approach: The drive itself is easy — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek Trailhead, about 28 miles total — but the climb to Cathedral Peak is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state. From the trailhead, the Andrews Creek Trail (#504) climbs roughly 12 miles to 6,680+ ft Andrews Pass, then descends into the Spanish Creek drainage before a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lakes below the peak's southwest side, putting the one-way approach at around 18 miles with significant elevation gain and loss along the way. Most parties treat this as a 2-4 day backpack (roughly 40+ miles round trip), camping at or near Cathedral Lakes before making a summit push. A free self-issue wilderness permit is required at the trailhead, along with a trailhead parking pass; the first many miles are a hot, rocky, buggy uphill slog with little shade, so this is genuinely a remote, multi-day alpine objective rather than a day-approach crag. For this specific route: from Cathedral Lakes camp, follow the trail toward Cathedral Pass and climb scree/talus to the base of the peak's main South Face; SE Buttress starts on the left wall just after entering the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk, while NE Ridge is gained by continuing up and around toward the ridgeline running north.
